newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine business critical of labor pact - paper.
newsitem.headline: Argentine business critical of labor pact - paper.

text.p: Disappointed Argentine business leaders criticized a package of labor law reforms which the government agreed with unions and will send to Congress, according to the La Nacion newspaper Wednesday.

"It is a shame that we haven't been able to set an example to society by having business and unions agreeing on labor reform," said Jorge di Fiori, head of the Argentine Chamber of Commerce and a member of the powerful Group of Eight (G-8) business lobbies.

La Nacion quoted another, unidentified member of the G-8, who spoke in stronger terms: "Basically there was never a chance to negotiate anything. The unions were never willing to compromise on anything and they were feeling brave about it because their stance was backed by the government."

President Carlos Menem said Tuesday that he would send to Congress a slightly modified Act of Agreement which the government had previously agreed on with the CGT labor federation as a package of labor reforms.

Although business was able to persuade unions to include the creation of an unemployment insurance fund to replace the current compensation system for dismissal, the G-8 refused to sign the accord and will send Congressmen its own suggestions on labor reform.
The G-8 is calling for Congress to allow bigger companies to opt out of industry-wide collective bargaining and negotiate wage contracts directly with their unions.

The business group also called for employer contributions to a new unemployment fund to be limited to only 2.5 percent of wages -- and not the 4.0 percent in the union accord -- and for private health funds to be able to compete with union health funds.
The government desperately needs good news on the 17.3 percent unemployment rate ahead of October's mid-term elections in Congress.

The International Monetary Fund recommended labor reforms as a way of reducing employment costs and Menem tried last year to push a tough reform package through by decree. Blocked by courts and hostile unions, he tried three-way talks but the effort proved futile.
Late last month, Menem went behind the backs of business leaders to sign the Act of Agreement with unions, a watered down reform package.
